questions.q: What does torch.autocast do during a training step?
options: Converts every tensor in the model permanently to float16
Runs eligible ops like matmuls and convolutions in reduced precision while keeping sensitive ops like softmax and loss reductions in FP32
Replaces the optimizer with a faster low-precision version
Only affects tensors created on the CPU
questions.explain: autocast is a context manager that selectively casts operations: numerically safe, compute-heavy ops run in reduced precision, while sensitive reductions stay in FP32 for stability.

questions.q: Why is a GradScaler typically used with FP16 autocast but not with BF16 autocast?
options: GradScaler only works with FP16 tensors by API restriction
FP16's narrow range makes small gradients prone to underflowing to zero; BF16's FP32-like range mostly avoids that
BF16 does not support backward() at all
GradScaler is deprecated and should never be used
questions.explain: FP16 gradients can underflow to zero before reaching the optimizer, so GradScaler scales the loss up before backward and down before the step. BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range, so this is rarely needed.

questions.q: In the standard AMP + GradScaler training step, what is the correct order of calls?
options: optimizer.step() -> scaler.scale(loss).backward() -> scaler.update()
scaler.scale(loss).backward() -> scaler.step(optimizer) -> scaler.update()
scaler.update() -> loss.backward() -> optimizer.step()
loss.backward() -> scaler.update() -> scaler.step(optimizer)
questions.explain: The scaled loss is backpropagated first, then scaler.step() unscales gradients and calls the optimizer (skipping the step if it finds inf/nan), then scaler.update() adjusts the scale factor for the next iteration.

questions.q: What is the main practical difference between torch.cuda.amp.autocast() and the newer torch.autocast(device_type=...)?
options: The newer API is device-agnostic (CUDA, CPU, etc.) via a device_type argument, while the legacy API is CUDA-only
The newer API no longer supports float16
The legacy API runs faster on all hardware
They behave identically with no difference at all
questions.explain: torch.cuda.amp.autocast() is the older, CUDA-specific form. torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=...) is the unified, device-agnostic API that PyTorch now recommends, though the legacy form still works.

questions.q: If scaler.step(optimizer) detects an inf or nan in the gradients for that iteration, what happens?
options: Training crashes immediately with a RuntimeError
The optimizer step is skipped for that iteration and the scale factor is adjusted
The model weights are reset to their initial values
Nothing — inf and nan gradients are applied normally
questions.explain: GradScaler monitors for inf/nan gradients (a sign the current scale factor is too aggressive). When found, it skips that optimizer step and reduces the scale factor rather than corrupting the weights.
